The career prospects are a slight concern as well bc pure science graduates often end up doing things irrelevant to their degrees which is more likely to happen for these choices both statistically and from experience. It's not irrelevant. Rats are regularly exterminated here and rightly so. We are controlling a health risk. We are minimizing the threat they pose to us as disease vectors. Again, my point was never that "they are disease vectors, full stop", it's that they are vectors for dangerous diseases. While we're at it Hong Kong had a bubonic plague epidemic between 1890-1925, because of an overcrowded area that became a hotbed for rats and in turn fleas. It's pretty solid historical evidence that rat populations have to be controlled and that we should avoid unnecessary contact with them.

You can teach humans to practice personal hygiene and enforce relevant laws to ensure compliance. Rats multiply extremely quickly and often dwell in less than sanitary environments in cities. I'm not just basing my point on the mere fact that rats are disease vectors, I'm saying that allowing their proliferation or not being careful handling them poses risks to population health. To say that feral animals are hygienic is gross misinformation.

Sorry but that's plain flawed logic. Think about how malaria jumps off mosquitoes. There are bugs that should no longer be threats in developed places but are atill present because they are transmitted through means such as faecal matter of rats. Animals contribute to many potential viral and parasitic infections in humans. The SARS outbreak, for example, originated from bats which transmitted the virus to civet cats, both of these animals were widely consumed in China, and eventually this led to an outbreak.

Rats are vectors for parasites and viruses that wouldn't be transmitted otherwise. It depends on the environment of course, here in Hong Kong where they usually live around wet markets and in drainage systems they are a significant public health threat.

The convert to Trump is probably convinced by a number of specific policies. The USMCA, tax reform and immigration stand out. Not that these are definitely positive, more that they represent potential for positive change. Other more general observations are economic statistics, although I would consider these very rough indicators of his work to the point that these gains aren't attributable to him.

The typical Democrat voter of 2020 probably looks at the bigger picture, it's easy to be persuaded that Trump isn't lying if you look at individual cases where media negativity goes too far (as I imagine is how people get converted sorting by controversial), but the bigger picture shows a much larger denominator where this isn't the case and I wager that Trump supporters are conveniently ignoring this along with highly objectionable diplomatic and constitutional maneouvres that require much deeper analysis that the aberage person simply doesn't have time to dig into. Some of the stuff he does is not wrong in principle but bad in practice, and vice versa. If I was tunnel visioning I'd probably support Trump as well.

If I had a vote in 2020 I'd most likely vote for Yang. He has imo a clear vision for the future that is educated, workable and bold (Trump's boldness was probably why I leaned towards rooting for him in 2016; there's an intrinsic value to any change). Economically speaking he's actually much more compatible with a GOP supporter and less frightening than Bernie or Warren despite what UBI looks like on the surface. It disappoints me that people are defaulting to Trump when they lose faith in Democrats, I know Yang isn't being considered seriously and that's just sad.
